analysis.one_liner: Lets banks, securities firms, and insurance companies merge into single financial conglomerates.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 343 to 86 on July 1, 1999, but the Senate never voted on this version; its repeal of Glass-Steagall became law that November in the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill tears down the Depression-era Glass-Steagall walls that kept banks, securities firms, and insurance companies in separate businesses, and creates "financial holding companies" that can own all three at once, funded partly by insured deposits. It also preempts many state laws that restricted bank-insurance combinations, relaxes Federal Reserve oversight of nonbank affiliates, and requires banks to let customers opt out of having their personal information shared with third parties. The House passed it by a wide bipartisan margin, but the Senate never took it up; the merged version enacted later in 1999 as the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act carried the same core change.
analysis.who_benefits: The largest banks, securities firms, and insurers, which gain the ability to merge into diversified conglomerates that can take insured deposits, underwrite securities, and sell insurance from the same corporate family. Consumers get smaller, real benefits: mandatory disclosure of ATM fees at the machine, new federal rules against tricking people into disclosing their financial records, and notice before a bank shares their personal information.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Glass-Steagall provisions that barred a member bank from affiliating with a securities firm and barred interlocking directors between banks and securities firms.

Creates financial holding companies that may engage in any activity the Federal Reserve determines to be financial in nature, including insurance, securities underwriting, and lending, so long as their banks are well capitalized and well managed.
Requires ATM operators that charge fees to disclose them to the customer at the time of service, and directs a study of whether disclosure should come before the transaction is irrevocably committed.
Makes it a federal violation, with civil and criminal penalties, to obtain a financial institution's customer information under false pretenses.

Requires public meetings when regulators consider mergers of banks with $1 billion or more in assets, and directs annual reports on market concentration in financial services and its impact on consumers.

analysis.who_pays: Bank customers and depositors bear the tradeoffs: personal information can be shared with outside companies unless the customer affirmatively objects after receiving notice, state laws that restricted bank-insurance combinations are preempted, Federal Reserve power to police nonbank affiliates is narrowed, and deposit-insurance funds sit behind conglomerates that now hold riskier securities businesses. Community banks face new competition from the largest combinations, and independent insurance agents lose market share to banks selling insurance at the teller line.

drawbacks.text: Privacy protection is opt-out: a financial institution may disclose a customer's nonpublic personal information to nonaffiliated third parties unless the customer, after receiving notice, takes steps to prevent it.
The bill preempts state anti-affiliation laws and limits state regulation of insurance activities by banks and their affiliates, overriding stricter state consumer protections in many cases.

The Federal Reserve is barred from taking enforcement action against a nonbank holding-company subsidiary unless an unsafe practice poses a material risk to an affiliated bank or the payment system, sharply narrowing umbrella oversight.
It repeals the Federal Reserve's authority to restrict bank loans secured by stock, restrictions that had aimed at preventing the undue use of bank loans to speculate in securities.

Enforcement actions requiring an insurance or securities affiliate to shore up an affiliated bank become unenforceable if the SEC or a state insurance regulator says in writing that the action would materially hurt the affiliate's finances.

The bill itself directs a study of the projected impact on financial institutions with assets of $100 million or less and on insurance agents and consumers, an acknowledgment that smaller players and agents bore costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer-facing pieces—ATM fee disclosure, penalties for pretexting, privacy notices—are real but modest. The central change is structural: it lets the largest financial firms combine deposit-taking, securities underwriting, and insurance under preemption of many state rules, with privacy as an opt-out and weaker Federal Reserve backstop oversight. On balance the bill's gains flow overwhelmingly to the biggest financial firms, and the costs in consumer protection and systemic risk fall on customers and taxpayers backing deposit insurance.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 343 to 86, but the Senate simply placed it on its calendar on July 12, 1999, and never voted on it; the core repeal of Glass-Steagall was enacted that November as the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act after the House and Senate merged their competing bills.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill on July 1, 1999, by a recorded vote of 343 to 86, with 205 of 223 Republicans and 138 of 211 Democrats voting yes.

Democrats attempted two procedural moves on July 1 to stall or change the bill: a motion that the Committee of the Whole rise failed 179 to 232 (with 178 of 211 Democrats in favor and no Republicans), and a motion to recommit the bill with instructions failed 198 to 232 (196 of 211 Democrats in favor, 1 of 223 Republicans).
The bill was received in the Senate on July 12, 1999, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar under General Orders; no vote ever occurred on this version.

The substance of H.R. 10—the repeal of Glass-Steagall and the financial holding company framework—became law in November 1999 as the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, after House and Senate versions were merged in conference.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large financial conglomerates came out ahead: even though this exact bill died on the Senate calendar, its central change—repealing Glass-Steagall—was enacted later that year, and the House had already passed it with a big bipartisan majority, giving the merger of banking, securities, and insurance the congressional endorsement the industry had sought for decades.

sides.party_line_note: Passage was bipartisan—205 of 223 Republicans and 138 of 211 Democrats voted yes—but the attempts to delay or change the bill split almost perfectly by party: on the failed motion to recommit, 196 of 211 Democrats voted yes and 1 of 223 Republicans did.

industries.note: They can now combine insured deposit-taking with securities underwriting and insurance under one holding company, and state anti-affiliation laws are preempted. The cost to customers comes in weaker privacy defaults, narrower Federal Reserve oversight of nonbank arms, and greater concentration.

They gain access to bank deposits and the ability to affiliate with banks, while bank securities activities are brought under securities-law registration. Consumers gain some investor-protection rules but lose the separation between insured deposits and securities risk.

Insurers gain the ability to affiliate with and even acquire banks, with many state restrictions preempted, but they also face new competition as banks begin selling insurance products—national banks are barred from underwriting most insurance as principal, preserving the industry's underwriting role.
Banks can now cross-sell insurance at the point of a loan, taking a distribution channel agents previously controlled; the bill itself orders a study of the impact on insurance agents and consumers.

They face competition from the largest new conglomerates, but the bill expands Federal Home Loan Bank eligibility and allows advances for small business, agriculture, rural development, and low-income community lending, and directs a study of the impact on institutions with $100 million or less in assets.
Operators that charge fees must now disclose them to customers at the machine, a modest compliance cost paired with a real consumer benefit.
